\chapter{Preguntó Dónde --- What the Accent Was Always For}
\label{ch:pregunto-donde}
\hlchaptermodality{215}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can report a question that begins with an asking word, accent intact.}

I can report a question that begins with an asking word, accent intact.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[preguntó dónde]{preguntó dónde}

\label{lesson:ES-C57-pregunto-donde}



\begin{quote}
Report a yes-or-no question. (\emph{Preguntó si trabajaba}.)

Now one that cannot be answered with yes or no: \emph{¿Dónde trabaja?}
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the asking word is the joint}]
\begin{quote}
\emph{¿Dónde trabaja?} \emph{\textbf{Preguntó dónde trabajaba.}}
\end{quote}

No \emph{que}. No \emph{si}. The asking word \textbf{is} the joint — it was already at the front of the question, and it stays there.

The rest is what you already do: question marks gone, verb stepped back into the imperfect.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{culture}
Now look at \emph{dónde} in that reported sentence. \textbf{The accent is still there} — in a sentence with no question marks at all.

This is the answer to a question you may have been carrying since the sixth chapter. The accent was never a partner to the question marks. It marks the word as an \textbf{asking} word, and the asking is still inside the report: he wanted to know something, and \emph{dónde} is the something.

Compare the two jobs the same letters can do:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\emph{donde} & plain — it just points at a place \\
\emph{\textbf{dónde}} & asking — it wants the place named \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The marks around a sentence tell you the \emph{sentence} is a question. The accent on a word tells you the \emph{word} is doing the asking. Those are different facts, and only now do you have a sentence where one is true and the other is not.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Preguntó dónde trabajaba}
  \item \emph{Preguntó si trabajaba}, then \emph{Preguntó dónde trabajaba}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What joins the report when the question starts with an asking word? (\textbf{The asking word itself} — no \emph{que}, no \emph{si}.)

And what does the accent on \emph{dónde} mark? (That the \textbf{word} is asking — not that the sentence is a question.)
\end{tcolorbox}
